exercises.objective: Explain the exploration/exploitation tradeoff in the bandit setting.
exercises.prompt: In the multi-armed bandit problem, choosing an action $a_t$ has two simultaneous effects on your future performance. Name both effects, and explain with a concrete scenario why a policy that always plays $\operatorname*{argmax}_a\hat\mu_a$ (the empirically best arm so far) can perform badly in the long run.
hints: The two effects: it collects reward now (exploitation), and it collects information/data about that arm, improving your future knowledge (exploration).

Concrete scenario: suppose arm A gave a lucky high reward on your very first (and only) try, while arm B (actually better on average) gave one unlucky low reward on its first try. Pure exploitation would lock onto A forever, since $\hat\mu_A>\hat\mu_B$ from that point on, never trying B again to discover it's actually better.

This is exactly why exploration matters: without ever revisiting under-tried arms, you can get permanently stuck on a suboptimal arm based on early noise, this is the core failure mode UCB1 is designed to avoid by explicitly tracking confidence, not just the point estimate.

exercises.objective: Compute a UCB1 score for a bandit arm.
exercises.prompt: After $n=20$ total rounds, an arm has been played $n_a=5$ times with empirical mean $\hat\mu_a=0.3$. Using $\beta=1$, compute its UCB1 score $\hat\mu_a+\beta\sqrt{2\ln n/n_a}$. Enter a decimal to 3 decimal places.

exercises.objective: Explain how the GP posterior formulas relate to the Gaussian conditioning identity and the ridge-regression closed form.
exercises.prompt: The GP posterior mean $\mu(x|D)=\kappa(x)^\top(K+\sigma_0^2I)^{-1}y$ is obtained by treating $(f(x),y_1,..,y_n)$ as one big jointly-Gaussian vector and applying PROB-05's Gaussian conditioning identity. Explain (a) why the joint vector $(f(x),y_{1:n})$ is Gaussian at all (what GP property guarantees this), and (b) why $\sigma_0^2$ (the observation noise variance) gets added to $K$'s diagonal specifically, rather than appearing elsewhere.
hints: (a) By the GP definition itself: for *any* finite set of input points (here, the query point $x$ together with the $n$ training inputs), the corresponding function values are defined to be jointly Gaussian. So $(f(x),f(x_1),..,f(x_n))$ is Gaussian by construction, and adding independent Gaussian observation noise to each $f(x_i)$ (giving $y_i$) keeps the whole vector Gaussian (sums of jointly Gaussian and independent-Gaussian variables are still jointly Gaussian).

(b) $y_i=f(x_i)+\text{noise}$, with the noise independent across data points and independent of $f$ itself. The covariance of $y_i$ with itself is $\text{Cov}(f(x_i),f(x_i))+\text{Var}(\text{noise}) = k(x_i,x_i)+\sigma_0^2$ (the noise variance adds only to the diagonal, since the noise terms for different $i$ are independent of each other and don't affect the off-diagonal covariances $k(x_i,x_j)$ between different training points).

This is exactly why $(K+\sigma_0^2I)$ appears instead of plain $K$: it's the covariance matrix of the *observed* $y$'s (not the noise-free $f$'s), and only the diagonal changes, since observation noise at different points is assumed independent.

exercises.objective: Compute a GP posterior mean at a query point given precomputed kernel quantities.
exercises.prompt: For data $x=(0,1)$, $y=(1,2)$, squared-exponential kernel $k(x,x')=\exp(-0.5(x-x')^2)$, noise $\sigma_0=0.1$, and query $x^*=0.5$: $\kappa(x^*)=(0.8825,0.8825)$, and $(K+\sigma_0^2I)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1.5483&-0.9298\\-0.9298&1.5483\end{pmatrix}$ (both precomputed for you). Compute $\mu(x^*|D)=\kappa(x^*)^\top(K+\sigma_0^2I)^{-1}y$. Enter a decimal to 2 decimal places.
hints: $= 0.8825\times(2.1668-0.3113) = 0.8825\times1.8555 \approx 1.64$. Note this sits between the two observed $y$-values (1 and 2), closer to $y_2=2$ (the point $x_2=1$ is at the same kernel-distance from $x^*=0.5$ as $x_1=0$ here, so the pull is symmetric in kernel terms, but the posterior mean is a genuinely correlated blend, not a simple average, illustrating why GPs are called 'Bayesian kernel ridge regression').

exercises.objective: Compare the behavior of the three standard acquisition functions.
exercises.prompt: MPI only integrates the probability mass beyond $y^*$ (current best), while EI additionally weights that mass by $(y^*-y)$ (how much better), and UCB uses $\mu_D(x)+\beta\sigma_D(x)$ directly. Explain why MPI can behave poorly compared to EI (hint: think about a point with a tiny probability of a huge improvement vs. a point with a large probability of a tiny improvement), and what increasing $\beta$ does to UCB's exploration/exploitation balance.
hints: MPI treats 'any improvement, however small' the same as 'a huge improvement', as long as the probability of exceeding $y^*$ is the same. So MPI can favor a point offering a high probability of a negligible improvement over a point offering a lower probability of a massive improvement, which is usually the wrong choice for actually finding the true optimum.

EI fixes this by weighting the probability of improvement by the SIZE of that improvement, $(y^*-y)$, so a low-probability-but-huge-improvement point can outscore a high-probability-but-tiny-improvement one, generally a better-behaved criterion for global optimization.

For UCB, larger $\beta$ up-weights the uncertainty term $\sigma_D(x)$ relative to the mean $\mu_D(x)$, pushing the acquisition function to favor genuinely unexplored regions (more exploration); smaller $\beta$ makes it favor regions already believed to be good (more exploitation), exactly the same explore/exploit dial as the bandit setting's $\beta$ in UCB1.
